summary:
Martian Map is an interactive map prototype for planning a Marswalk in two sites in Gale Crater. It was built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge and its challenge "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map."

The map combines NASA-provided CTX imagery and elevation data with derived slope, roughness, and route information. The habitat and science-target coordinates are placeholders. This is a demonstration project, not an operational navigation or astronaut-safety system.
details:
Martian Map

Martian Map is an interactive map for planning a walk on the surface of Mars. It shows four areas of Gale Crater, each 5 km by 5 km. The map is made from real NASA data: a 1 meter elevation model and CTX satellite images.

A Python program reads the elevation data and works out how steep the ground is. It marks the cells that are too steep or too rough as hazards. The red overlay on the map is hazard detection overlay.

The user clicks on the map to add checkpoints. Checkpoints can be dragged to a new place or deleted. Every time the checkpoints change, the app finds a new walking route that starts at the habitat, visits each checkpoint in order and returns to the habitat. The route never goes through a hazard cell (strictly programmed to not give a path through hazard points), and a safety margin setting keeps it a set distance away from hazards.

The user can choose the pathfinding method: A*, Dijkstra or Weighted A*. The app also shows route options for the same checkpoints, such as the fastest route and alternatives. Each option shows its time, distance and distance from hazards.

A safety summary shows the route distance, the EVA (spacewalk) time, the time left after returning, and whether the plan is within the EVA time limit. A readout shows the position and map cell under the cursor.

BENEFITS

The map shows the terrain, the hazards, and the route at one place and the time limit and checkpoints in a separate panel which can be expanded for control. A planner can see unsafe sites, route times (ETA), and how much EVA time is left after the return. Changing a checkpoint updates everything immediately; many plans can be tried quickly.

INTENDED IMPACT

The project is meant to help crews and mission planners work out safe walking routes for Mars surface trips. Adding a new site only needs a clip of the elevation data and an entry in the configuration file.

TOOLS

- Languages: Python 3, JavaScript, HTML and CSS

- Libraries and software: NumPy, rasterio and GDAL for the data; Leaflet for the map; A*, Dijkstra and Weighted A* written in JavaScript

- Version control: Git and GitHub

- AI coding assistants helped write and review the code (listed in the Use of AI section)

- Hardware: a standard laptop

- Data: NASA Gale Crater DEM (Digital Elevation Map) and CTX imagery

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Users can test their own paths by clicking on locations to add checkpoints, drag them to move them, and delete them. Each time we change one, the app finds a new route and shows it.

For each plan, the app lists route options with their time, distance and distance from hazards, so you can pick the one that suits the mission. We can choose the pathfinding method, and the app shows how long it took and how many map cells it checked. You can also change the safety margin.

We chose four sites with different ground: a flat crater floor, a steep southern area, and two rough areas. The project also runs automatic checks. One check makes sure no route crosses a hazard cell. Another makes sure the pathfinding methods find routes of matching cost.

Every assumption and placeholder in the app is labeled, so the user knows which numbers come from data and which are estimates.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Safety: hazard cells cannot be entered, the safety margin keeps routes away from them, and the walk back is always counted in the EVA time.

- Data: the data has a limited resolution, and the surrounding map is labeled as lower resolution and for context only.

- Assumptions: walking speed, EVA length, the slope limit and the radiation dose rate are labeled assumptions, not NASA limits. The habitat and the science targets are placeholders. (all assumptions mentioned in README.md & config.py)

- Missing data: radiation and weather measurements are not part of the route finding yet, and the app says so.

- Speed: large data files are read in small pieces, and the route is calculated in the browser so it updates immediately.

- Reuse: all data processing is done by scripts (src), so a site can be rebuilt from the raw files.
